claim: Side population (SP) cells were found at a frequency higher than 0.01% in 36 out of 64 lymph node (LN) biopsies (53.12%).
source: We found an SP population at a frequency higher than 0.01% in 36 out of 64 LN biopsies (53.12%).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from analysis of human LN biopsies showing the frequency of SP cells.

claim: The content of SP cells in lymph nodes correlated with the histological diagnosis.
source: However, the content of SP cells in the LN did correlate with the LN histological diagnosis.
evidence: The manuscript states a correlation between SP cell content and histological diagnosis based on analysis of patient samples.

claim: The accumulation of SP cells was significantly higher in LN from lymphadenitis patients than in lymphoma patients.
source: The accumulation of SP cells was significantly higher in LN from lymphadenitis patients than in lymphoma patients.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative data between patient groups showing statistical differences.

claim: Follicular lymphadenitis (FL) and granulomatous lymphadenitis (GL) LN contained a median of 0.2% SP cells with a range from <0.01% to ~40%.
source: Interestingly, FL and GL LN contained a median of 0.2% SP cells with a range from <0.01% to ~40%, which was significantly higher than the content of SP cells in VL, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma LN (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements from patient samples and references supporting figures.

claim: Human and murine side population (SP) cells are enriched in long-term reconstituting HSC and other more committed populations of progenitors.
source: Human and murine SP cells, with ability to extrude the dye Hoechst 33342 through upregulated activity of multidrug resistance protein complexes (Zhou et al., 2001) in BM and other tissues (Brusnahan et al., 2010; Challen and Little, 2006; Goodell et al., 1996), are enriched in long-term reconstituting HSC and other more committed populations of progenitors (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Weksberg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work establishing this characteristic of SP cells.

claim: LN SP cells from patients with reactive lymphadenitis were capable of producing myeloid colonies in CFU assays.
source: To confirm whether LN SP cells indeed contained HSC/P, we first sorted LN SP cells from patients with reactive lymphadenitis and plated them in methylcellulose cultures containing rhIL-3, rhIL-6, and rhSCF cytokines. CFU analysis demonstrated that SP cells were indeed capable of producing myeloid colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), while non-SP cells were devoid of measurable CFU-forming ability (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental CFU assays performed on sorted patient cells with results shown in referenced figure.

claim: Non-SP cells from lymph nodes were devoid of measurable CFU-forming ability.
source: CFU analysis demonstrated that SP cells were indeed capable of producing myeloid colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), while non-SP cells were devoid of measurable CFU-forming ability (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results comparing SP and non-SP cells.

claim: The vast majority of CD45+/CD34+ cells co-expressed CD133+.
source: The vast majority of CD45+/CD34+ cells co-expressed CD133+, and the CD45+/CD34- population was split ~50:50 into CD133+ and CD133- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides immunophenotypic analysis data with specific percentages from flow cytometry.

claim: Adult inflammatory LN tissues contain an increased number of myeloid-committed HSC/P.
source: In combination, these data show the accumulation of a myeloid-committed HSC/P population in human lymphadenitis. Adult inflammatory LN tissues therefore contain an increased number of myeloid-committed HSC/P.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: The release of HSC/P from BM into the bloodstream follows circadian cycles.
source: The release of HSC/P from BM into the bloodstream follows circadian cycles (Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2008) controlled by the activity and fate of inflammatory cells (Casanova-Acebes et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LPS induced upregulation of HSC/P in peripheral blood peaking at ZT10, 6 hr post-administration.
source: In our experiments, the circadian mobilization pattern of HSC/P in the PB was severely modified by the administration of LPS, with the increase in HSC/P appearing later and peaking at ZT10, 6 hr post-administration (Figure 1C), coincident with an increased neutrophil count in the PB (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental time-course data from LPS-treated mice with specific time points.

claim: LPS administration resulted in increased neutrophil count in peripheral blood at ZT10.
source: In our experiments, the circadian mobilization pattern of HSC/P in the PB was severely modified by the administration of LPS, with the increase in HSC/P appearing later and peaking at ZT10, 6 hr post-administration (Figure 1C), coincident with an increased neutrophil count in the PB (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing neutrophil counts at specific time points.

claim: LPS did not elicit a significant change in the level of splenic HSC/P within the first 12 hr after inflammation.
source: Interestingly, LPS did not elicit a significant change in the level of splenic HSC/P within the first 12 hr after inflammation (Esplin et al., 2011; Wright et al., 2001; Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from spleen analysis with supporting citations.

claim: The BM HSC/P content decreased with a nadir occurring as early as 3 hr after LPS administration (at ZT7).
source: The BM HSC/P content decreased, which supports the migratory nature of the increased HSC/P in the PB (Figure 1H); yet the nadir of the BM HSC/P content occurred as early as 3 hr after LPS administration (at ZT7), returning to normal values by 6 hr (ZT10, Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript provides time-course data showing changes in BM HSC/P content.

claim: The lymphatic circulation in LPS-treated animals showed a significant increase in the levels of circulating HSC/P in the LN and the thoracic duct.
source: Indeed, the lymphatic circulation in LPS-treated animals did show a significant increase in the levels of circulating HSC/P in the LN and the thoracic duct compared to controls that closely mirrored the decline of HSC/P in the BM (Figure 1I, J).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental measurements from lymphatic tissues showing increased HSC/P.

claim: LPS induced expansion of BM LSK and immunophenotypically identified LT-HSC, ST-HSC, and MPP populations at later time points (Z10–ZT16).
source: LPS induced expansion of BM Lin-/c-kit+/Sca-1+ (LSK) and immunophenotypically identified long-term (LT)-HSC, short-term (ST)-HSC, and multipotential progenitors (MPPs) populations at later time points (Z10–ZT16) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-K) with no changes in the BM HSC content by ZT7, suggesting a differential effect of LPS signaling on the HSC population.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data showing changes in specific HSC populations over time.

claim: The GMP population was significantly decreased by ZT7 after LPS administration.
source: Interestingly, the reduction in the BM content of progenitors was not homogenous throughout the hematopoietic progenitor populations. Confirming the egress of BM CFU-GM described above, the GMP population was significantly decreased by ZT7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, K), while the content of immunophenotypically defined common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) only declined by ZT10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, L), and the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (MEP) content was increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, M), resulting in no significant net changes in the content of BM Lin-/c-kit+/Sca1- (LK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, N).
evidence: The manuscript provides flow cytometry data showing temporal changes in specific progenitor populations.

claim: The content of immunophenotypically defined CMPs only declined by ZT10 after LPS administration.
source: Confirming the egress of BM CFU-GM described above, the GMP population was significantly decreased by ZT7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, K), while the content of immunophenotypically defined common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) only declined by ZT10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, L), and the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (MEP) content was increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, M), resulting in no significant net changes in the content of BM Lin-/c-kit+/Sca1- (LK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, N).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal flow cytometry data for CMP populations.

claim: The MEP content was increased after LPS administration.
source: Confirming the egress of BM CFU-GM described above, the GMP population was significantly decreased by ZT7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, K), while the content of immunophenotypically defined common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) only declined by ZT10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, L), and the megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (MEP) content was increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, M), resulting in no significant net changes in the content of BM Lin-/c-kit+/Sca1- (LK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, N).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data showing increased MEP content.

claim: Inflamed LN did not contain increased levels of repopulating cells by ZT7.
source: The analysis of competitive repopulating units (CRUs) in the LN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) demonstrated that inflamed LN did not contain increased levels of repopulating cells by ZT7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from competitive repopulation assays.

claim: LN contained a transient, short-term myelopoietic progenitor population without medium- or long-term multilineage repopulation ability.
source: LN contained a transient, ST-myelopoietic progenitor population without medium- or long-term multilineage repopulation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional characterization of LN progenitors through repopulation assays.

claim: LN SP cells from LPS-treated mice are enriched in LK cells and depleted in LSK cells.
source: Furthermore, LN SP cells from LPS-treated mice are enriched in LK cells and depleted in LSK cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry analysis of SP cells from LN.

claim: LN SP cells contain exclusively short-term repopulating progenitors with the ability to differentiate into myeloid cells.
source: LN SP cells contain exclusively ST-repopulating progenitors with the ability to differentiate into myeloid cells (data not shown) and are depleted from any significant 8–16 weeks engrafting HSC, as assessed using CRU assays (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G), unlike their BM SP counterparts that are enriched in LSK cells and LT-repopulating activity (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, H).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional characterization through CRU assays.

claim: BM SP cells are enriched in LSK cells and long-term repopulating activity.
source: LN SP cells contain exclusively ST-repopulating progenitors with the ability to differentiate into myeloid cells (data not shown) and are depleted from any significant 8–16 weeks engrafting HSC, as assessed using CRU assays (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G), unlike their BM SP counterparts that are enriched in LSK cells and LT-repopulating activity (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, H).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of BM SP cells through flow cytometry and CRU assays.

claim: LPS induces a selective lymphatic circulation of myeloid committed progenitors, but not other types of HSC/P populations.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that LPS induces a selective lymphatic circulation of myeloid committed progenitors, but not other types of HSC/P populations.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: Bone lymphatic endothelial cells arise rapidly from pre-existing regional lymphatics upon osteoclast activation.
source: Recently, bone lymphatic endothelial cells have been shown to arise rapidly from pre-existing regional lymphatics in inducible bone-expressing Vegfc transgenic mice through Vegfr3, osteoclast activation, and bone loss (Hominick et al., 2018; Monroy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Acute endotoxemia is associated with osteoclast activation and bone loss.
source: Acute endotoxemia is associated with osteoclast activation and bone loss (Hardy and Cooper, 2009; Nason et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The homing of Lin- cells to the BM in mice treated with LPS was reduced by ~65% compared with vehicle-treated counterparts.
source: The homing of cells to the BM in mice treated with LPS was reduced by ~65% compared with their vehicle-treated counterparts (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative homing assay data comparing LPS and control treatments.

claim: The bone of LPS-treated animals contains a Lyve1+ network, which was only rarely identified in PBS-treated mice.
source: Lyve1eGFP knock-in mice revealed that the bone of LPS-treated animals contains a Lyve1+network, which was only rarely identified in PBS-treated mice (Figure 2D), suggesting that LPS-induced inflammation may upregulate the expression of the hyaluronan receptor Lyve1 and render patent a pre-existing network of Lyve1+bone cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations from transgenic reporter mice.

claim: LPS-induced inflammation may upregulate the expression of the hyaluronan receptor Lyve1 and render patent a pre-existing network of Lyve1+ bone cells.
source: Lyve1eGFP knock-in mice revealed that the bone of LPS-treated animals contains a Lyve1+network, which was only rarely identified in PBS-treated mice (Figure 2D), suggesting that LPS-induced inflammation may upregulate the expression of the hyaluronan receptor Lyve1 and render patent a pre-existing network of Lyve1+bone cells.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on observed data, indicating speculation.

claim: Lin-/DiI+ homed cells were located closer to the endosteum in response to LPS at as early as 1.5 hr after administration of LPS.
source: Interestingly, Lin-/DiI+ homed cells were located closer to the endosteum in response to LPS at as early as 1.5 hr after administration of LPS (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy data showing spatial localization of labeled cells.

claim: The seeding of BM-derived Lin-/DiI+ cells into LN increased approximately threefold after LPS administration.
source: On the other hand, the seeding of BM-derived Lin-/DiI+ cells into LN increased approximately threefold, which mirrored the decline in BM homing (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from cell tracking experiments.

claim: The migrated HSP/C are spatially positioned in the cortex area surrounding primary follicles in LN.
source: Histological analysis of BM-derived Lin-/DiI+ cells within the LN by confocal microscopy showed that the migrated HSP/C are spatially positioned in the cortex area surrounding primary follicles (Figure 2I), consistent with localization in T-cell zone for antigen presentation.
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy data showing spatial distribution of cells in LN.

claim: The rapid egress of hematopoietic progenitors from BM during inflammation may occur through bone lymphatics draining into LN.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the rapid egress of hematopoietic progenitors from BM during inflammation may indeed occur through bone lymphatics draining into LN.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple observations to propose a mechanism, indicating inference.

claim: The majority of the differentially accumulated myeloid progenitors in LN by 3 hr post-administration of LPS were granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (CFU-GM).
source: The majority of the differentially accumulated myeloid progenitors in LN by 3 hr post-administration of LPS were granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (CFU-GM) and in a much lesser degree unipotent granulocyte progenitors (GPs, CFU-G) with no differential accumulation of unipotent macrophage progenitors (MPs, CFU-M) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data characterizing progenitor types in LN.

claim: LPS induced differential donor-derived specific GMP differentiation toward the formation and retention of cDC in LN.
source: We found that LPS induced differential donor-derived specific GMP differentiation toward the formation and retention of cDC in LN (Figure 3C), but not in the BM (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: The content of macrophages and granulocytes did not significantly change with LPS in either LN or BM.
source: The content of macrophages and granulocytes did not significantly change with LPS in either LN or BM (Figure 3C, D), confirming the specific nature of the lymphoid-tissue cDC differentiation of mobilized GMP in LPS-treated mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data showing no significant changes in specific cell populations.

claim: LPS administration resulted in an approximately threefold accumulation of CD115++/Flt3++ cells in LN.
source: Serial gating of lineage-/Cx3cr1-GFP++/c-Kitint cells (Figure 3E, P2) showed an approximately threefold accumulation of CD115++/Flt3++ cells in LN and a concomitant 65% depletion in the BM as early as 3 hr after LPS administration (Figure 3F, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data showing changes in MDP populations.

claim: LPS administration resulted in a concomitant 65% depletion of CD115++/Flt3++ cells in the BM as early as 3 hr after administration.
source: Serial gating of lineage-/Cx3cr1-GFP++/c-Kitint cells (Figure 3E, P2) showed an approximately threefold accumulation of CD115++/Flt3++ cells in LN and a concomitant 65% depletion in the BM as early as 3 hr after LPS administration (Figure 3F, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data showing temporal changes in BM MDP populations.

claim: LPS-induced systemic inflammation results in robust and specific recruitment of phenotypic GMP that are BM cDC-committed progenitors to the LN.
source: In the absence of significant changes in the LN content of macrophages, these data demonstrate that LPS-induced systemic inflammation results in robust and specific recruitment of phenotypic GMP that are BM cDC-committed progenitors to the LN.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: Immune cells and HSC/P express TLR.
source: Immune cells and HSC/P express TLR (Beutler and Rietschel, 2003; Nagai et al., 2006; Takeuchi and Akira, 2010), which act as microorganism sensors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LPS stimulation of TLR recruits MyD88 and TRIF through the canonical and endosomal pathways, respectively.
source: LPS stimulation of TLR recruits MyD88 and TRIF through the canonical and endosomal pathways, respectively. Both adaptors subsequently recruit TRAF6, which acts as the molecular hub of both signaling branches (Akira et al., 2001; Kawai and Akira, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work describing TLR signaling pathways.

claim: TRAF6 acts as the molecular hub of both MyD88 and TRIF signaling branches.
source: LPS stimulation of TLR recruits MyD88 and TRIF through the canonical and endosomal pathways, respectively. Both adaptors subsequently recruit TRAF6, which acts as the molecular hub of both signaling branches (Akira et al., 2001; Kawai and Akira, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The deficiency of Traf6 in hematopoietic cells completely abrogated the LPS-induced increase in CFU-GM frequency in LN.
source: LN from Mx1Cre;WT chimeric mice after LPS administration (at ZT7, corresponding with the peak of progenitor content in LN, Figure 1H) revealed a threefold increase in the frequency of CFU-GM. This increase was completely abrogated by the deficiency of Traf6 in hematopoietic cells (Mx1Cre;Traf6Δ/Δ animals, Figure 4B), indicating that the signals that result in CFU-GM mobilization to LN are mediated by hematopoietic Traf6.
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data from genetic knockout experiments.

claim: The signals that result in CFU-GM mobilization to LN are mediated by hematopoietic Traf6.
source: This increase was completely abrogated by the deficiency of Traf6 in hematopoietic cells (Mx1Cre;Traf6Δ/Δ animals, Figure 4B), indicating that the signals that result in CFU-GM mobilization to LN are mediated by hematopoietic Traf6.
evidence: The manuscript infers mechanism from genetic knockout data.

claim: The cell-autonomous deficiency of Traf6 resulted in a relative decrease in migration of ~40% of BM myeloid progenitors in the presence of LPS.
source: We found that the cell-autonomous deficiency of Traf6 resulted in a relative decrease in migration of ~40% (Figure 4D) of BM myeloid progenitors in the presence of LPS, indicating that Traf6 is required for LPS-dependent cell-autonomous BM myeloid progenitor migration.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from transwell migration assays.

claim: Traf6 is required for LPS-dependent cell-autonomous BM myeloid progenitor migration.
source: We found that the cell-autonomous deficiency of Traf6 resulted in a relative decrease in migration of ~40% (Figure 4D) of BM myeloid progenitors in the presence of LPS, indicating that Traf6 is required for LPS-dependent cell-autonomous BM myeloid progenitor migration.
evidence: The manuscript infers requirement from genetic knockout data.

claim: LN-derived cells generated more potent chemoattractant signals, resulting in a much larger migration of WT BM myeloid progenitors (fivefold higher, ~30%) during the same period.
source: Interestingly, analysis of non-cell-autonomous migration of BM myeloid progenitors demonstrated that LN-derived cells generated more potent chemoattractant signals, resulting in a much larger migration of WT BM myeloid progenitors (fivefold higher, ~30%) during the same period (Figure 4E, F), which was drastically diminished (~50% reduction) by Traf6-deficiency in LN cells, but not when using control BM cells as chemoattractant source (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from transwell migration assays comparing different cell sources.

claim: Traf6-deficiency in LN cells resulted in ~50% reduction in migration of BM myeloid progenitors.
source: Interestingly, analysis of non-cell-autonomous migration of BM myeloid progenitors demonstrated that LN-derived cells generated more potent chemoattractant signals, resulting in a much larger migration of WT BM myeloid progenitors (fivefold higher, ~30%) during the same period (Figure 4E, F), which was drastically diminished (~50% reduction) by Traf6-deficiency in LN cells, but not when using control BM cells as chemoattractant source (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from transwell migration assays with Traf6-deficient cells.

claim: The chemoattractant gradient generated by LPS on LN cells is the predominant effect responsible for Traf6-dependent myeloid progenitor migration.
source: These data indicate that although LPS-mobilized myeloid progenitors depend on both cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous Traf6-dependent signals, the chemoattractant gradient generated by LPS on LN cells is the predominant effect responsible for Traf6-dependent myeloid progenitor migration.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes migration assay data to reach this conclusion.

claim: The non-cell-autonomous effect does not seem to be due to secretion of the chemokine inducer IFN-γ.
source: Interestingly, the non-cell-autonomous effect does not seem to be due to secretion of the chemokine inducer IFN-γ, which was not detectable in LN-derived supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), strongly suggesting that activated LN NK cells may not be responsible for the migration of BM myeloid progenitors.
evidence: The manuscript reports cytokine measurement data showing absence of IFN-γ.

claim: Activated LN NK cells may not be responsible for the migration of BM myeloid progenitors.
source: Interestingly, the non-cell-autonomous effect does not seem to be due to secretion of the chemokine inducer IFN-γ, which was not detectable in LN-derived supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), strongly suggesting that activated LN NK cells may not be responsible for the migration of BM myeloid progenitors.
evidence: The manuscript infers lack of NK cell involvement from absence of IFN-γ.

claim: The effect of Traf6 expression on non-cell-autonomous, LN-mediated migration did not depend on the secretion of IL-1α, IL-2, IL-13, IL-4, TNF-α, or IL-10 regulatory cytokines.
source: And, similarly, the effect of Traf6 expression on non-cell-autonomous, LN-mediated migration did not depend on the secretion of IL-1α, IL-2, IL-13, IL-4, TNF-α, or IL-10 regulatory cytokines of inflammatory processes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports cytokine measurement data showing no dependence on specific cytokines.

claim: LN CD11b+ cells from Traf6Δ/Δ mice can recapitulate the same reduction of progenitor migration achieved by complete LN tissue.
source: Although only ~1% of LN cells are myeloid, we observed that LN CD11b+ cells, but not B- or T-cells, from Traf6Δ/Δ mice can recapitulate the same reduction of progenitor migration achieved by complete LN tissue (Figure 4H).
evidence: The manuscript reports transwell migration assay data using sorted cell populations.

claim: Mature myeloid lineage-specific deletion of Traf6 abrogated the migration of myeloid progenitors to LN in response to LPS.
source: Mature myeloid lineage-specific deletion of Traf6 abrogated the migration of myeloid progenitors to LN in response to LPS (Figure 4I).
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data from Lyz2Cre;Traf6 conditional knockout mice.

claim: Deficiency of Traf6 in mature myeloid lineage-specific cells resulted in an increase in the endotoxemia-dependent mortality.
source: A major consequence of the deficiency of Traf6 in mature myeloid lineage-specific cells was an increase in the endotoxemia-dependent mortality (Figure 4J), indicating that Traf6 expression in mature myeloid cells is required for both migration of myeloid progenitors to LN and protection of LPS-induced mortality.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival data from conditional knockout mice.

claim: Traf6 expression in mature myeloid cells is required for both migration of myeloid progenitors to LN and protection of LPS-induced mortality.
source: A major consequence of the deficiency of Traf6 in mature myeloid lineage-specific cells was an increase in the endotoxemia-dependent mortality (Figure 4J), indicating that Traf6 expression in mature myeloid cells is required for both migration of myeloid progenitors to LN and protection of LPS-induced mortality.
evidence: The manuscript infers requirement from genetic knockout and survival data.

claim: LPS/Traf6 signaling is required for migration of myeloid progenitors through predominantly long-range acting, mature myeloid lineage-dependent chemoattractant signals.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that LPS/Traf6 signaling is required for migration of myeloid progenitors through predominantly long-range acting, mature myeloid lineage-dependent chemoattractant signals, and that LPS/Traf6 signaling in Lyz2-expressing cells is protective against endotoxin-induced inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: LPS/Traf6 signaling in Lyz2-expressing cells is protective against endotoxin-induced inflammation.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that LPS/Traf6 signaling is required for migration of myeloid progenitors through predominantly long-range acting, mature myeloid lineage-dependent chemoattractant signals, and that LPS/Traf6 signaling in Lyz2-expressing cells is protective against endotoxin-induced inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes survival and migration data to reach this conclusion.

claim: Activation of TLRs conserves inflammatory pathways that culminate in the activation of the NF-κB transcription factors.
source: Activation of TLRs conserves inflammatory pathways that culminate in the activation of the NF-κB transcription factors (Karin and Greten, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The expression of IκBαSR does not reduce the effect of LPS on the migration of myeloid progenitors toward LPS-stimulated macrophages/cDC.
source: Analysis of LPS-driven migration in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J) demonstrated that the expression of IκBαSR does not reduce the effect of LPS on the migration of myeloid progenitors toward LPS-stimulated macrophages/cDC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L), indicating that NF-κB transcription factors are dispensable for myeloid progenitor migration.
evidence: The manuscript reports transwell migration assay data using cells expressing IκBα super-repressor.

claim: NF-κB transcription factors are dispensable for myeloid progenitor migration.
source: Analysis of LPS-driven migration in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J) demonstrated that the expression of IκBαSR does not reduce the effect of LPS on the migration of myeloid progenitors toward LPS-stimulated macrophages/cDC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L), indicating that NF-κB transcription factors are dispensable for myeloid progenitor migration.
evidence: The manuscript infers dispensability from IκBα super-repressor experiments.

claim: Inhibition of intracellular protein traffic using monensin dramatically decreased myeloid precursor migration.
source: In contrast, inhibition of intracellular protein traffic using monensin dramatically decreased myeloid precursor migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L), suggesting that intracellular protein trafficking is necessary for the migration phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript reports transwell migration assay data using monensin treatment.

claim: Intracellular protein trafficking is necessary for the migration phenotype.
source: In contrast, inhibition of intracellular protein traffic using monensin dramatically decreased myeloid precursor migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L), suggesting that intracellular protein trafficking is necessary for the migration phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript infers necessity from monensin inhibition experiments.

claim: LPS-induced myeloid progenitor migration occurs through an NF-κB-independent, intracellular protein traffic-dependent pathway.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that LPS-induced myeloid progenitor migration occurs through an NF-κB-independent, intracellular protein traffic-dependent pathway, and suggests that the progenitor-mobilizing effect of LPS may not require transcriptional activation, depending rather on the intracellular traffic of secreted proteins.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: The progenitor-mobilizing effect of LPS may not require transcriptional activation, depending rather on the intracellular traffic of secreted proteins.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that LPS-induced myeloid progenitor migration occurs through an NF-κB-independent, intracellular protein traffic-dependent pathway, and suggests that the progenitor-mobilizing effect of LPS may not require transcriptional activation, depending rather on the intracellular traffic of secreted proteins.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on experimental data, indicating speculation.

claim: LPS induced upregulation of Cxcl12 expression in BM, but not in LN.
source: However, by ZT7, LPS induced upregulation of Cxcl12 expression in BM, but not in LN, indicating that Cxcl12 tissue concentrations per se could not explain the mechanism of migration to LN (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports ELISA data measuring Cxcl12 levels in different tissues.

claim: Cxcl12 tissue concentrations per se could not explain the mechanism of migration to LN.
source: However, by ZT7, LPS induced upregulation of Cxcl12 expression in BM, but not in LN, indicating that Cxcl12 tissue concentrations per se could not explain the mechanism of migration to LN (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript infers lack of mechanism from differential tissue expression data.

claim: LPS induced upregulation of several myeloid cell cytokines and chemokines in the extracellular fluid of LN rather than BM as early as 1 hr after LPS challenge.
source: As expected, LPS induced upregulation after administration of several myeloid cell cytokines and chemokines with ability to recruit and differentiate macrophages and cDC in the extracellular fluid of LN rather than BM as early as 1 hr after LPS challenge (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–J).
evidence: The manuscript reports multiplex cytokine array data from tissue samples.

claim: In vivo administration of LPS promotes a secretion of Ccl19 in LN when compared with BM and PB.
source: Analysis of Ccl19 in the extracellular fluid of the femoral cavity, LN, and plasma demonstrated that in vivo administration of LPS promotes a secretion of Ccl19 in LN when compared with BM and PB (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports ELISA data measuring Ccl19 levels in different tissues.

claim: Ccl21 did not show the formation of similar differential tissue concentrations in LN after LPS administration.
source: This differential secretion is specific to Ccl19 since Ccl21, a highly related chemokine, did not show the formation of similar differential tissue concentrations in LN after LPS administration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports ELISA data comparing Ccl19 and Ccl21 levels.

claim: Ccl19 is secreted by LN myeloid cells after LPS stimulation and depends on Traf6 expression.
source: Ccl19 is secreted by LN myeloid cells after LPS stimulation and depends on Traf6 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports ELISA data from sorted cell populations with and without Traf6.

claim: Ccr7-mediated signals control the migration of immune cells to secondary lymphoid organs such as LN.
source: Ccr7-mediated signals control the migration of immune cells to secondary lymphoid organs such as LN, facilitating efficient surveillance and targeted cellular response (Förster et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: LPS upregulates membrane Ccr7 expression on cDC and their committed progenitors.
source: Also, LPS upregulates membrane Ccr7 expression on cDC and their committed progenitors (Schmid et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: In vivo neutralization of Ccl19 resulted in a dramatic reduction (>90%) in the number of CFU-GM in the LN of LPS-treated animals by ZT7.
source: We found a dramatic reduction (>90%) in the number of CFU-GM in the LN of LPS-, anti-Ccl19-treated animals by ZT7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data from antibody neutralization experiments.

claim: Ccr7-expressing GMP in BM rapidly decreased in response to LPS and increased in regional draining LN chains.
source: Also, we confirmed that Ccr7-expressing GMP in BM rapidly decreased in response to LPS and increased in regional draining LN chains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data tracking Ccr7+ GMP in different tissues.

claim: The abrogation of accumulation of progenitors in LN was reproduced by the administration of anti-Ccr7.
source: The abrogation of accumulation of progenitors in LN was reproduced by the administration of anti-Ccr7 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data from antibody neutralization experiments.

claim: Membrane Ccr7 levels were significantly upregulated as early as 1 hr after LPS administration on GMP in LPS-treated WT mice.
source: Membrane Ccr7 levels were significantly upregulated as early as 1 hr after LPS administration on GMP in LPS-treated WT mice. Such upregulation was abrogated in LPS-treated Traf6-deficient GMP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data measuring Ccr7 expression on GMP.

claim: Ccr7 upregulation on GMP was abrogated in LPS-treated Traf6-deficient GMP.
source: Membrane Ccr7 levels were significantly upregulated as early as 1 hr after LPS administration on GMP in LPS-treated WT mice. Such upregulation was abrogated in LPS-treated Traf6-deficient GMP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from Traf6-deficient cells.

claim: Hematopoietic chimeric Ccl19-/- animals did not mount a migratory response of myeloid progenitors from BM to LN in response to LPS.
source: Finally, we confirmed that hematopoietic chimeric Ccl19-/- animals did not mount a migratory response of myeloid progenitors from BM to LN in response to LPS (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data from Ccl19 knockout chimeric mice.

claim: The rapid migration of BM myeloid progenitors to LN depends on the expression of the chemokine Ccl19 and its receptor Ccr7.
source: Together, these data indicate that the rapid migration of BM myeloid progenitors to LN depends on the expression of the chemokine Ccl19 and its receptor Ccr7.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: In vivo L-selectin blockade did not abrogate GMP migration to regional LN.
source: In these mice, in vivo L-selectin blockade did not abrogate GMP migration to regional LN while sinusoidal-dependent B-lymphocyte mobilization into regional LN was significantly impaired (Figure 5H, I), indicating that the migration of BM myeloid progenitors, unlike B-cells, into the regional lymphatic circulation is L-selectin independent and therefore unlikely to be mediated by LN high endothelial venules (Rosen, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from antibody blockade experiments.

claim: Sinusoidal-dependent B-lymphocyte mobilization into regional LN was significantly impaired by L-selectin blockade.
source: In these mice, in vivo L-selectin blockade did not abrogate GMP migration to regional LN while sinusoidal-dependent B-lymphocyte mobilization into regional LN was significantly impaired (Figure 5H, I), indicating that the migration of BM myeloid progenitors, unlike B-cells, into the regional lymphatic circulation is L-selectin independent and therefore unlikely to be mediated by LN high endothelial venules (Rosen, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from antibody blockade experiments.

claim: The migration of BM myeloid progenitors into the regional lymphatic circulation is L-selectin independent.
source: In these mice, in vivo L-selectin blockade did not abrogate GMP migration to regional LN while sinusoidal-dependent B-lymphocyte mobilization into regional LN was significantly impaired (Figure 5H, I), indicating that the migration of BM myeloid progenitors, unlike B-cells, into the regional lymphatic circulation is L-selectin independent and therefore unlikely to be mediated by LN high endothelial venules (Rosen, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript infers L-selectin independence from antibody blockade experiments.

claim: The migration of BM myeloid progenitors is unlikely to be mediated by LN high endothelial venules.
source: In these mice, in vivo L-selectin blockade did not abrogate GMP migration to regional LN while sinusoidal-dependent B-lymphocyte mobilization into regional LN was significantly impaired (Figure 5H, I), indicating that the migration of BM myeloid progenitors, unlike B-cells, into the regional lymphatic circulation is L-selectin independent and therefore unlikely to be mediated by LN high endothelial venules (Rosen, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript infers mechanism from L-selectin independence data with supporting citation.

claim: Ccl19/Ccr7 chemokine signaling is required for the rapid migration of myeloid progenitors to LN upon LPS administration.
source: Altogether, these data strongly indicated that Ccl19/Ccr7 chemokine signaling is required for the rapid migration of myeloid progenitors to LN upon LPS administration.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to reach this conclusion.

claim: There was an increase in the levels of PS residues on the outer membrane leaflet of WT LN cDC2 (defined as CD11b+/CD11c+), but not in the CD11b-/CD11c+ population.
source: We found an increase in the levels of PS residues on the outer membrane leaflet of WT LN cDC2 (defined as CD11b+/CD11c+), but not in the CD11b-/CD11c+ population, which comprises cDC1 and plasmacytoid DC (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data measuring annexin-V binding to PS.

claim: The exposure of PS residues was abrogated in Traf6∆∕∆ LN cDC.
source: Interestingly, the exposure of PS residues was abrogated in Traf6∆∕∆ LN cDC (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from Traf6-deficient cells.

claim: Traf6 mediates the process of vesicle exocytosis.
source: Given that Traf6 deficiency does not modify the survival of hematopoietic cells or progenitors (Fang et al., 2018; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), our observations on annexin-V binding indicate that Traf6 mediates the process of vesicle exocytosis.
evidence: The manuscript infers mechanism from annexin-V binding data and prior published work.

claim: Increased myeloid progenitor migration was reversed by specific inhibitors for Irak1/4, Ubc13, and IKKβ.
source: Increased myeloid progenitor migration was reversed by all three specific inhibitors (Figure 6B), indicating that the integrity of canonical signaling pathway upstream of NF-κB might be required to attract myeloid progenitors from the BM to the LN.
evidence: The manuscript reports transwell migration assay data using pharmacological inhibitors.

claim: The integrity of canonical signaling pathway upstream of NF-κB might be required to attract myeloid progenitors from the BM to the LN.
source: Increased myeloid progenitor migration was reversed by all three specific inhibitors (Figure 6B), indicating that the integrity of canonical signaling pathway upstream of NF-κB might be required to attract myeloid progenitors from the BM to the LN.
evidence: The manuscript infers requirement from inhibitor experiments, indicating speculation.

claim: Phospho-SNAP23(Ser95) is significantly upregulated by LPS in LN cDC.
source: Phospho-SNAP23(Ser95) is significantly upregulated by LPS in LN cDC (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data measuring phospho-SNAP23 levels.

claim: Each of the inhibitors for Irak1/4, Ubc13, and IKK abrogated the activation of SNAP23.
source: Each of the inhibitors for Irak1/4, Ubc13, and IKK abrogated the activation of SNAP23 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data from cells treated with inhibitors.

claim: The activation through Traf6/Irak1/4/Ubc13 induced by LPS activates vesicular fusion and vesicular cargo release of pre-formed Ccl19 accumulated in late endosomes of LN myeloid cells.
source: Altogether, this set of data indicates that the activation through Traf6/Irak1/4/Ubc13 induced by LPS activates vesicular fusion and vesicular cargo release of pre-formed Ccl19 accumulated in late endosomes of LN myeloid cells.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to propose a mechanism.

claim: A subpopulation of cDC but not pDC or macrophages contained most of the cytoplasmic expression of Ccl19.
source: Analysis of steady-state LN myeloid cell populations identified a subpopulation of cDC but not pDC or macrophages, containing most of the cytoplasmic expression of Ccl19.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry analysis of intracellular Ccl19.

claim: B220-/CD8- cDC that expressed CD205+ and CD172a+ distinctly stored high levels of cytosolic Ccl19.
source: Further analysis of the subpopulations of LN cDC2 demonstrated that B220-/CD8- cDC that expressed the endocytic receptor DEC-205 (CD205+) and the mannose receptor signal regulatory protein α (SIRPα, CD172a+) distinctly stored high levels of cytosolic Ccl19 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) unlike other DC populations, which expressed low levels of intracellular Ccl19 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data measuring intracellular Ccl19 in specific DC subsets.

claim: A subpopulation of cDC2 stores intracellular Ccl19 and is potentially able to self-regulate the migration of its own progenitors in inflammation.
source: These data indicate that a subpopulation of cDC2 stores intracellular Ccl19 and is potentially able to self-regulate the migration of its own progenitors in inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript infers potential function from intracellular Ccl19 storage data, indicating speculation.

claim: This study describes a previously unrecognized, rapid, emergent traffic of myeloid progenitor cells from the BM via lymphatic vessels directly to lymphatic tissues that bypass the peripheral blood stream.
source: This study describes a previously unrecognized, rapid, emergent traffic of myeloid progenitor cells from the BM via lymphatic vessels directly to lymphatic tissues that bypass the peripheral blood stream.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The lymphatic-mediated traffic from BM is highly activated in endotoxic inflammation and drains into regional LN chains.
source: Although the exact anatomical and functional nature of this lymphatic network in the bone remains poorly defined, our data demonstrate that the lymphatic-mediated traffic from BM is highly activated in endotoxic inflammation and drains into regional LN chains.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings about lymphatic traffic.

claim: As early as 90 min after LPS administration myeloid progenitors are in closer proximity to the lymphatic endothelium in BM.
source: Our data showed that as early as 90 min after LPS administration myeloid progenitors to or are in closer proximity to the lymphatic endothelium in BM while 1.5 hr later there is an ~70% reduction of myeloid progenitors within the BM and a marked increase of myeloid progenitors in the LN tissue.
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal microscopy and quantification data.

claim: 1.5 hr after LPS administration there is an ~70% reduction of myeloid progenitors within the BM and a marked increase of myeloid progenitors in the LN tissue.
source: Our data showed that as early as 90 min after LPS administration myeloid progenitors to or are in closer proximity to the lymphatic endothelium in BM while 1.5 hr later there is an ~70% reduction of myeloid progenitors within the BM and a marked increase of myeloid progenitors in the LN tissue.
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal quantification data from multiple tissues.

claim: Two temporally distinct waves of progenitors take place, a fast one to the lymphatic circulation followed by a slower one into the blood stream.
source: This observation, along with the need of a longer period of time to detect an increase in the frequency of myeloid progenitors in peripheral blood, suggests that two temporally distinct waves of progenitors take place, a fast one to the lymphatic circulation followed by a slower one into the blood stream.
evidence: The manuscript infers two waves from temporal distribution data.

claim: The administration of a single dose of LPS suffices to induce migration of GMP/MDP while no other types of progenitors or stem cells migrate to lymphatics in this first wave of egression.
source: In our study, by using transgenic animals, we demonstrated that the administration of a single dose of LPS suffices to induce migration of GMP/MDP while no other types of progenitors or stem cells migrate to lymphatics in this first wave of egression before any significant contribution from or to PB and differentiate into short-lived LN cDCs in a murine acute model of inflammatory signaling by LPS, and that therefore they may modulate the course of infectious diseases and other inflammatory conditions.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings from transgenic mouse studies.

claim: GMP/MDP differentiate into short-lived LN cDCs in a murine acute model of inflammatory signaling by LPS.
source: In our study, by using transgenic animals, we demonstrated that the administration of a single dose of LPS suffices to induce migration of GMP/MDP while no other types of progenitors or stem cells migrate to lymphatics in this first wave of egression before any significant contribution from or to PB and differentiate into short-lived LN cDCs in a murine acute model of inflammatory signaling by LPS, and that therefore they may modulate the course of infectious diseases and other inflammatory conditions.
evidence: The manuscript reports differentiation data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: This traffic is rapid, before LPS induces proliferation and/or apoptosis.
source: This traffic of myeloid progenitors from BM to LN is rapid, before LPS induces proliferation and/or apoptosis (Nagai et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2014), and can be recapitulated in mice receiving intrafemoral adoptive transfer of GMPs.
evidence: The manuscript describes timing of traffic relative to other LPS effects with supporting citations.

claim: GMP/MDP tend to localize in the T-cell areas of LN.
source: These GMP/MDP tend to localize in the T-cell areas of LN.
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy data showing spatial localization.

claim: No significant mobilization of M-CSF-responding monocyte progenitors (CFU-M) can be found as early as 3 hr after LPS administration.
source: No significant mobilization of M-CSF-responding monocyte progenitors (CFU-M) can be found as early as 3 hr after LPS administration before any significant effect of LPS on proliferation may take place.
evidence: The manuscript reports CFU assay data showing no change in CFU-M.

claim: The interference of this traffic by blocking Traf6-dependent signaling in Lyz2-expressing myeloid cells results in increased animal death.
source: Interestingly, the interference of this traffic by blocking Traf6-dependent signaling in Lyz2-expressing myeloid cells results in increased animal death.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival data from conditional knockout mice.

claim: Ccr7+ GMP/MDP, but not other myeloid or lymphoid progenitors, egress BM.
source: Ccr7+ GMP/MDP, but not other myeloid or lymphoid progenitors, egress BM.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes flow cytometry and functional data showing selective egress.

claim: The progenitor traffic to the systemic lymphatic circulation is mediated by Ccl19/Ccr7.
source: The progenitor traffic to the systemic lymphatic circulation is mediated by Ccl19/Ccr7 and is NF-κB independent, Traf6/IκB-kinase/SNAP23 activation dependent, and is responsible for the secretion of pre-stored Ccl19 by a subpopulation of CD205+/CD172a+ conventional dendritic cells type 2 and upregulation of BM myeloid progenitor Ccr7 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes multiple experimental findings demonstrating the mechanism.

claim: The progenitor traffic is NF-κB independent.
source: The progenitor traffic to the systemic lymphatic circulation is mediated by Ccl19/Ccr7 and is NF-κB independent, Traf6/IκB-kinase/SNAP23 activation dependent, and is responsible for the secretion of pre-stored Ccl19 by a subpopulation of CD205+/CD172a+ conventional dendritic cells type 2 and upregulation of BM myeloid progenitor Ccr7 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript reports data from IκBα super-repressor experiments showing NF-κB independence.

claim: The progenitor traffic is Traf6/IκB-kinase/SNAP23 activation dependent.
source: The progenitor traffic to the systemic lymphatic circulation is mediated by Ccl19/Ccr7 and is NF-κB independent, Traf6/IκB-kinase/SNAP23 activation dependent, and is responsible for the secretion of pre-stored Ccl19 by a subpopulation of CD205+/CD172a+ conventional dendritic cells type 2 and upregulation of BM myeloid progenitor Ccr7 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript reports data from genetic and pharmacological experiments showing pathway dependence.

claim: A subpopulation of CD205+/CD172a+ conventional dendritic cells type 2 is responsible for the secretion of pre-stored Ccl19.
source: The progenitor traffic to the systemic lymphatic circulation is mediated by Ccl19/Ccr7 and is NF-κB independent, Traf6/IκB-kinase/SNAP23 activation dependent, and is responsible for the secretion of pre-stored Ccl19 by a subpopulation of CD205+/CD172a+ conventional dendritic cells type 2 and upregulation of BM myeloid progenitor Ccr7 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data identifying the cell population storing Ccl19.

claim: Mature myeloid Traf6 signaling is anti-inflammatory and necessary for lymph node myeloid cell development.
source: Mature myeloid Traf6 signaling is anti-inflammatory and necessary for lymph node myeloid cell development.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival and differentiation data from conditional knockout mice.
